turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_process_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3
    cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and `target` (the measured yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa)).
  - b3_htsteel_process_pool.csv: 34 CANDIDATE samples whose yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST yield
strength at room temperature (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from
the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

**1. What the pool contains.** All 34 candidates are variants of a ~13 wt% Cr martensitic stainless steel (three closely related compositions: ~0.2 C with 0.6 Ni / 0.2 Ti / no Ni), austenitized at 1010–1050 °C. The only meaningful differences are the **Heat treatment step 2 (tempering) temperature** (200–740 °C) and the presence/parameters of a final aging step.

**2. Dominant trend in the training set: tempering temperature.** For quench-and-temper martensitic steels in the training data, yield strength rises sharply as the tempering (stage 2) temperature drops below ~550 °C:

- 83.7275 Fe / 11.25 Cr alloy: temper 550 °C → 1090 MPa; 400 °C → 1340 MPa; 200 °C → 1330 MPa
- 82.95 Fe / 11.25 Cr alloy: temper 650 → 750; 600 → 910; 500 → 1190; 475 → 1430 MPa
- 83.845 Fe / 13 Cr / 0.4 C: temper 500 °C → 1390 MPa vs 600 °C + aging → 820–840 MPa
- 84.125 Fe / 13 Cr / 0.12 C + Ti: temper 540 → 780; 250 → 930 MPa
- 13 Cr steels tempered at 700–750 °C fall to only ~350–580 MPa; adding long low-temperature aging after high tempering drops them further (e.g., 370–430 MPa)

**3. Applying this to the pool.** All candidates share very similar composition and hardening chemistry (~0.2 C, 13 Cr), so the tempering temperature dominates:

- **200 °C temper:** c015 (no-Ni, 0.205 C variant), c021 (Ti-bearing variant) — expected ~900–1300 MPa
- **300 °C temper:** c018, c017 — expected ~900–1100 MPa
- **450–500 °C temper:** c014, c006, c004, c031 — still strong (~800–1000 MPa)
- **600 °C temper:** c016, c027 — moderate (~700–900 MPa)
- **700–740 °C temper (± aging):** the remaining ~24 candidates — soft (~400–700 MPa), since high-temperature tempering plus long aging consistently gave the lowest strengths for 13 Cr steels in training.

**4. Tie-breaking within temperature groups.** The 0.205 C no-Ni variant keeps all carbon available for martensite hardening (Ti in the other variant ties up ~0.05 C as TiC), so I rank it slightly above the Ti-bearing variant at the same tempering temperature.

**Selected top 5:** the two 200 °C candidates, the two 300 °C candidates, then the best 450 °C candidate.

Final: c015, c021, c018, c017, c014
